title: DFS, grids and connected components
overview: This module adds depth-first search, which goes as deep as possible before backing up, written with recursion. It then moves both BFS and DFS onto 2D grids, where each cell is a node, and uses DFS to count connected components and their sizes.

concepts.explain: Mark the node, then call `dfs` on each unvisited neighbour. The call stack remembers where to come back to.
Cell `(i, j)` is a node. Its neighbours are the 4 cells up, down, left and right, taken from a `direction` list of `{di, dj}` pairs.
Before touching a neighbour, check it is inside the grid: `0 <= i < n` and `0 <= j < m`. Then check it is not visited and not a wall.
Loop over every node; each time you find an unvisited one, start a DFS and add 1 to the count. Each DFS paints one whole piece.
Reset a counter before each DFS and increment it inside `dfs`; after the call it holds that component's size.
DFS on a grid that changes cell values as it goes, e.g. recolour every connected pixel of the same colour.

files.title: DFS traversal
files.what: Recursive DFS from node 0 that prints nodes in the order it enters them.
steps: Build the undirected adjacency list.
`dfs(src)` prints `src` and marks it visited.
For each unvisited `child`, call `dfs(child)` right away: go deep first.
When all children are done, the function returns to its caller (backtracking).
files.complexity: Time O(V + E) · Space O(V) for the recursion stack
files.input_note: `n e`, then edges. Tree: 0 has children 1 and 2; 1 has 3 and 4; 2 has 5.
files.output_note: `0 1 3 4 2 5`: the whole branch under 1 is finished before 2 is visited (BFS would print `0 1 2 3 4 5`).
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: What plays the role of BFS's queue in recursive DFS?

files.title: BFS on a 2D grid
files.what: Reads a grid, runs BFS from a source cell and prints the fewest steps to the destination cell.
steps: Read `n m` and the grid characters, then `si sj di dj`.
Queue holds `pair<int,int>` cells; `level[si][sj] = 0`.
For each popped cell try the 4 `direction`s; if `valid` and not visited, push it with `level + 1`.
Print `level[di][dj]`.
files.input_note: `n m`, n rows of characters, then source row/col and destination row/col.
files.output_note: Going from (0,0) to (2,3) in an open 3x4 grid prints `5` (2 down + 3 right).
files.watch_out: This version ignores the grid characters: walls are not blocked yet (the next file adds that). Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: In an open grid, what is the BFS distance between (r1,c1) and (r2,c2)?

files.title: BFS on a grid with walls
files.what: Same grid BFS, but a cell with `#` can never be entered.
steps: Everything as in the plain grid BFS.
Extra condition when pushing: `grid[ci][cj] != '#'`.
The answer is `level[di][dj]`, or -1 if the walls cut the destination off.
files.input_note: 3x4 grid with a wall column; go from (0,0) to (0,2), which is just two cells to the right but behind a wall.
files.output_note: Prints `6`: the path must go down around the wall and back up.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: What does the program print if the destination is completely surrounded by walls?
check.a: -1, because `level` was initialised to -1 and never updated.

files.title: DFS on a 2D grid
files.what: Recursive DFS over grid cells that prints each cell as it is entered.
steps: Read the grid and the start cell.
`dfs(si, sj)` prints the cell and marks it.
Try the directions in order right, left, up, down; recurse into each valid unvisited cell.
files.complexity: Time O(n·m) · Space O(n·m) recursion depth in the worst case
files.output_note: `0 0`, `0 1`, `0 2`, `1 2`, `1 1`, `1 0`: it runs right as far as it can, then down, then back left, like a snake.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why does the order of the `direction` list change the output?
check.a: DFS follows the first valid direction immediately, so the list order decides which way it goes first.

files.title: Count connected components
files.what: Starts a DFS from every node that is still unvisited; the number of starts is the number of components.
steps: Build the graph and clear `vis`.
Loop `i` from 0 to n-1.
If `vis[i]` is false, call `dfs(i)` (marks the whole piece) and do `count++`.
Print `count`.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: A graph has 10 nodes and no edges. How many components?
check.a: 10: every lonely node is its own component.

files.title: How many nodes can N reach?
files.what: DFS from N while counting how many nodes get visited.
steps: Build the graph and read `start_node`.
`dfs` does `count++` for every node it enters.
Print `count` after the DFS.
files.input_note: Graph from the problem; start at node 2 (its piece is {0,1,2,3}).
files.output_note: The real output is a compile error: `reference to 'count' is ambiguous`. The intended answer is `4`.
files.watch_out: Two bugs. (1) A global named `count` clashes with `std::count` because of `using namespace std;` - rename it, e.g. `cnt`. (2) `main` declares a new local `int count = 0;` that hides the global, so it would print 0 even after the rename. Delete that local line and print the global.

check.q: Why is naming a global `count` risky with `using namespace std`?
check.a: The standard library already has `std::count`, so the name becomes ambiguous.

files.title: Number of components (practice)
files.what: Same component-counting loop as the lesson, typed again as practice.
steps: Build graph, clear `vis`.
For each unvisited node: `dfs(i)` and `count++`.
Print the count.
files.input_note: 10 nodes but only a few edges, so nodes 7, 8, 9 are alone.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why must the loop go over **all** n nodes and not only nodes that appear in edges?
check.a: Isolated nodes never appear in an edge but still count as components.

files.title: Size of every component
files.what: Counts nodes inside each DFS, stores each size, sorts and prints them.
steps: Before each new DFS set `component_size = 0`.
`dfs` adds 1 for every node it visits.
Push the size into `sizes`, sort ascending, print.
files.complexity: Time O(V + E + k log k) · Space O(V)
files.input_note: Same 9-node graph as the lesson: pieces of size 4, 2 and 3.
files.watch_out: The space between numbers is commented out, so output reads `234` instead of `2 3 4`; print `sizes[i] << " "`. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.a: Just before each `dfs(i)` call in the loop, so each component starts counting from zero.

files.title: LeetCode 733 - Flood Fill
files.what: DFS from the start pixel that repaints every connected pixel having the original colour.
steps: If the start pixel already has the new colour, return the image unchanged (this also avoids endless recursion).
`dfs` sets the current pixel to `newColor`.
For each of the 4 neighbours inside the image whose colour equals `origColor`, recurse.
Repainted pixels no longer match `origColor`, so they act as their own visited marks.
files.input_note: Driver format: `n m`, the image, then `sr sc color`. This is LeetCode example 1.
files.output_note: The printed image is `2 2 2 / 2 2 0 / 2 0 1`, which matches LeetCode's expected output: the bottom-right 1 stays because it only touches the others diagonally.

check.q: Why is no `vis` array needed here?
check.a: A repainted pixel no longer has the original colour, so the colour check itself prevents revisiting (as long as new colour != old colour).

recap: DFS = mark, then recurse into each unvisited neighbour.
Grid cell = node; 4 directions; always check `valid` first.
BFS on a grid gives the fewest steps; DFS only explores.
Components: loop all nodes, start DFS on unvisited, count starts.
Avoid global names like `count` that clash with `std`.

check_yourself.q: What three checks guard a grid neighbour before you visit it?
check_yourself.a: Inside the grid (`valid`), not visited, and not a wall.

check_yourself.q: Can DFS find the shortest path in a grid?
check_yourself.a: Not in general; it finds *a* path. Use BFS for the shortest one.

check_yourself.q: How would you get the largest component instead of all sizes?
check_yourself.a: Keep `mx = max(mx, component_size)` after each DFS.
